title: Can AI break encryption? OpenAI’s new math has cryptographers divided
key_facts: OpenAI posted 722 AI-written maths manuscripts in one go; it withdrew three within a day.
Matthew Green of Johns Hopkins University suggested a 15 percent chance we could lose confidence in existing public-key encryption.
Yehuda Lindell (Bar-Ilan University, head of cryptography at Coinbase) says there is no evidence whatsoever of a breakthrough against the underlying problems.
Dan Boneh of Stanford calls it striking that none of the 722 papers deals with cryptography.

A preprint by Florian Tramer of ETH Zurich and colleagues, three at Anthropic, tested models on 191 code-breaking challenges; Anthropic says Claude found an improved attack on the HAWK signature scheme.
Govind Pimpale concedes that no currently deployed algorithm has been broken by AI; Bart Preneel says there is no real reason to panic.
quote_evidence: Today no currently deployed algorithm has been broken by AI,” Pimpale concedes.
“I think there is, at least at this moment, no real reason to panic,” he says.
why_it_matters_hint: Encryption secures banking and messaging, so even a hypothetical AI-found shortcut would matter, but nothing has been shown.
event_date: OpenAI release 6 Oct 2026; debate in the days after
notes: Full text read. The 6 Oct release date is from other outlets in the pool; the article says 'last week'.
